Mockolate is a modern, strongly-typed, AOT-compatible mocking library for .NET, powered by source generators. It enables fast, compile-time validated mocking with .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8, .NET 10 and .NET Framework 4.8. Source generator-based: No runtime proxy generation. Fast: Direct dispatch with no reflection or dynamic proxies. Strongly-typed: Compile-time safety and IntelliSense support. AOT compatible: Works with Native AOT and trimming. Modern C#: First-class support for ref structs, static interface members, and current language features. IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); bool success = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 4); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once();

The basics of creating, setting up and verifying mocks cover most tests. The following features help in the remaining cases: Feature Use it when you want to … Protected members set up or verify protected virtual members of a class mock Static interface members mock static abstract or static virtual interface members Advanced callback features control how often and when return values and callbacks apply Monitor interactions only verify the interactions within a scope, or reset the recorded interactions Check for unexpected interactions make sure every interaction was verified, or every setup was used Scenarios switch between sets of setups, for collaborators with an internal state For example, scenarios let a dispenser with a Refill method behave differently before and after a refill: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty").Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("loaded"); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true);

Returns, Throws and Do entries form a sequence: each call uses the next entry, and after the last entry the sequence starts over. The following modifiers change how an entry takes part in the sequence. They work on methods, properties, indexers and events alike. Modifier Effect .When(predicate) applies the entry only when the predicate on the invocation counter is true .For(n) uses the entry for n calls in a row before moving on .Only(n) uses the entry at most n times in total; .OnlyOnce() is short for .Only(1) .Forever() uses the entry for all further calls; the sequence no longer starts over .InParallel() runs a Do callback on every call, alongside the sequence

Execute a callback or return a value only when the zero-based invocation counter satisfies a predicate: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Called!")).When(count => count >= 2); // The first two calls are skipped

Use an entry for several calls in a row before moving on to the next one: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("First three calls")).For(3) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Next three calls")).For(3); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Returns(10).For(1) .Returns(20).For(2) .Returns(30).For(3); // Reads: 10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 30, 10, 20, 20, …

Stop using an entry after it was used a number of times: // Execute the callback up to 3 times dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Up to 3 times")).Only(3); // Throw only on the first read dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Throws(new Exception("This exception is thrown only once")).OnlyOnce() .Returns(42); // Reads: throws, 42, 42, 42, …

Mark the last entry with .Forever() to use it for all further calls instead of starting the sequence over: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true).For(2) // Returns true the first two times .Returns(false).Forever(); // Then always returns false

Multiple Do callbacks take turns, like the entries of a Returns sequence. Mark a callback with .InParallel() to run it on every call instead: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … call")) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on every call")).InParallel() .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … call")); .InParallel() only applies to Do callbacks, not to Returns or Throws.

Callbacks can receive the zero-based invocation counter as their first parameter: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do((count, type, amount) => Console.WriteLine($"Call #{count}: {amount} {type}")); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.OnGet .Do((count, value) => Console.WriteLine($"Read #{count}, value: {value}")); // Indexer setter: the counter, then the key(s), then the new value dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].OnSet .Do((count, type, newValue) => Console.WriteLine($"Set #{count}: this[{type}] = {newValue}"));

VerifyThatAllInteractionsAreVerified() returns true when every recorded interaction was matched by at least one verification. Use it to make sure that the code under test made no calls you didn't expect: dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Once(); bool allVerified = dispenser.Mock.VerifyThatAllInteractionsAreVerified(); // true

VerifyThatAllSetupsAreUsed() returns true when every setup was matched by at least one interaction. Use it to make sure that your test setup and the test execution match: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); bool allUsed = dispenser.Mock.VerifyThatAllSetupsAreUsed(); // false, the "Milk" setup was not used note Both methods return a bool instead of throwing, so assert the result with your test framework, for example Assert.True(allVerified).

A mock records all interactions from the moment it is created. To only verify the interactions within a given scope, use a monitor: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); MockMonitor<Mock.IMockVerifyForIChocolateDispenser> monitor = dispenser.Mock.Monitor(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Not monitored using (monitor.Run()) { dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 2); // Monitored } dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 3); // Not monitored // Verifications on the monitor only count the interactions while it was running monitor.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); MockMonitor<T> lives in the Mockolate.Monitor namespace. You can call monitor.Run() multiple times; each run adds to the monitored interactions.

For simpler scenarios, you can clear all recorded interactions of a mock with ClearAllInteractions(): IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Clears all previously recorded interactions dispenser.Mock.ClearAllInteractions(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 2); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); Setups are not affected by ClearAllInteractions().

Class mocks can also set up and verify protected virtual and abstract members. They work like public members, but are reached through Mock.SetupProtected, Mock.RaiseProtected and Mock.VerifyProtected: public abstract class ChocolateDispenser { protected virtual bool DispenseInternal(string type, int amount) => true; protected virtual int InternalStock { get; set; } protected virtual int this[int slot] { get => 0; set { } } } ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock();

// Set up a protected method dispenser.Mock.SetupProtected.DispenseInternal("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true); // Set up a protected property dispenser.Mock.SetupProtected.InternalStock.InitializeWith(100); All setup options of methods, properties and indexers are available.

// A protected method was called dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.DispenseInternal("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // A protected property was read and set dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.InternalStock.Got().AtLeastOnce(); dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.InternalStock.Set(100).Once(); // A protected indexer was read and set dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected[0].Got().Once(); dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected[0].Set(42).Once(); All verification options work the same as for public members.

Scenarios let you define multiple sets of setups on a single mock and switch between them at runtime. This is useful when the collaborator behaves differently depending on its internal state, for example a chocolate dispenser that starts empty, becomes loaded after Refill(…), and runs out of stock after dispensing: public interface IChocolateDispenser { bool Dispense(string type, int amount); bool Refill(int amount); } A mock always has an active scenario (the empty string "" by default). When a member is called, Mockolate looks for a matching setup in the active scenario first, and then in the default setups.

Use InScenario(name) to scope setups to a named scenario. Its Setup property mirrors dispenser.Mock.Setup, but the setups only apply while the scenario is active: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Throws<OutOfStockException>(); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true); A callback overload groups multiple setups of the same scenario: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded", scope => { scope.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); scope.Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); });

Chain .TransitionTo(name) on any method, property, indexer or event subscription setup to change the active scenario whenever the setup is used. The transition happens in addition to the return value or exception of the setup: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty") .Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("loaded"); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded") .Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("empty"); To set the starting state, change the active scenario directly with dispenser.Mock.TransitionTo("empty");.

When the mock is called, Mockolate looks for a matching setup in this order: The setups of the active scenario. The default setups (registered via dispenser.Mock.Setup). The mock's default behavior. Scenario setups add to the default setups instead of replacing them: register catch-all setups in the default scope and override specific members per scenario. Setups registered via InScenario never apply outside their scenario.

Mockolate supports mocking static abstract and static virtual members of interfaces (.NET 8+). They are set up, raised and verified like instance members, but through Mock.SetupStatic, Mock.RaiseStatic and Mock.VerifyStatic. C# only allows calls to static abstract members through a generic type parameter that is constrained to the interface, so code that uses them typically looks like this: public interface IChocolateFactory { static abstract string DefaultRecipe { get; set; } static abstract int ProduceBatch(string type, int amount); static abstract event Action<int> BatchCompleted; } public static class ChocolateProduction { public static string ReadRecipe<TFactory>() where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.DefaultRecipe; public static int Produce<TFactory>(string type, int amount) where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.ProduceBatch(type, amount); public static void Subscribe<TFactory>(Action<int> handler) where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.BatchCompleted += handler; } In the test, create the mock as usual and pass the generated mock type Mock.IChocolateFactory as the type argument: IChocolateFactory factory = IChocolateFactory.CreateMock(); // Set up static members factory.Mock.SetupStatic.ProduceBatch("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(42); factory.Mock.SetupStatic.DefaultRecipe.Returns("Dark"); // Call them through the generated mock type string recipe = ChocolateProduction.ReadRecipe<Mock.IChocolateFactory>(); // "Dark" int produced = ChocolateProduction.Produce<Mock.IChocolateFactory>("Dark", 10); // 42 ChocolateProduction.Subscribe<Mock.IChocolateFactory>(amount => Console.WriteLine($"Batch of {amount} ready")); // Raise static events factory.Mock.RaiseStatic.BatchCompleted(produced); // Verify static interactions factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.ProduceBatch("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.DefaultRecipe.Got().Once(); factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.BatchCompleted.Subscribed().Once();

Static calls are routed to the mock that was created last in the current async flow (internally an AsyncLocal). Tests that run in parallel therefore don't interfere with each other. warning Within a single test, create at most one mock per interface with static members. When you create a second mock of the same interface, all static calls are routed to the second mock.
Mockolate ships with Roslyn analyzers that catch mistakes at compile time. They are part of the Mockolate package, so there is nothing to install.

A verification without a count assertion. Verify methods only return a VerificationResult and do not throw on their own. You have to specify how often you expect the call to happen, e.g. .AtLeastOnce() or .Exactly(n), or use the verification result in another way. IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Mockolate0001: Add a count assertion like .AtLeastOnce() or use the result. dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()); The included code fix adds the .AtLeastOnce() count assertion: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).AtLeastOnce();

A type that cannot be mocked. This rule prevents you from mocking unsupported types: CreateMock(): the type must be an interface, a delegate or a class that can be derived from (e.g. not sealed). Implementing<T>(): the type must be an interface. It also fires when the type has a member that the mock would have to implement (an abstract member, or an interface member without a default implementation), but that your assembly cannot access: for example an internal abstract or private protected abstract member, or a { get; internal set; } property, on a type from a referenced assembly that does not grant InternalsVisibleTo. There is no valid code a mock could emit for such a member, so the type cannot be mocked at all. When a derived type already implements the inaccessible member The rule only considers members that the mock still has to implement. If a more derived type in the referenced assembly already overrides the inaccessible member, that type stays mockable: // In a referenced assembly that does not grant InternalsVisibleTo: public abstract class Dispenser { internal abstract void Refill(); } public abstract class ChocolateDispenser : Dispenser { internal override void Refill() { } } // Mockolate0002 fires for Dispenser, but ChocolateDispenser mocks fine. ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); Refill itself is not part of the mock, since your assembly cannot see it. An internal abstract override re-declaration does not count as an implementation, so the rule still fires for it. The same applies per accessor. For a property such as public abstract string Flavour { get; internal set; }, an override further down that implements the setter makes the type mockable. The mock then overrides the getter only, and Setup and Verify only offer the getter, since writes never reach the mock. See properties with only one accessor and indexers with only one accessor.

A member with a ref struct that Mockolate cannot set up. The mock still compiles and everything else on the type stays mockable, but the reported member gets no Setup or Verify members, and calling it throws a NotSupportedException. The rule fires in two situations. 1. The project does not meet the requirements for ref struct parameters Custom ref struct parameters (anything other than Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>) need a target framework of .NET 9 or later and C# 13 or later. Upgrade the target framework or <LangVersion> to resolve the warning. 2. The member uses a ref struct in a position that is never supported A method or delegate that returns a custom ref struct, a property of a custom ref struct type, or an indexer whose value is a custom ref struct. A delegate with a custom ref struct parameter, or with a ref readonly Span<T> / ref readonly ReadOnlySpan<T> parameter. Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> are supported everywhere else, both as parameters and as values. Virtual members of class mocks are not reported A virtual member of a mocked class keeps working: the mock forwards the call to the wrapped instance, or to the base class implementation, so there is nothing to fix. The forwarded call ignores the MockBehavior settings, because there is no setup to apply them to, and it is not recorded. Interface members, abstract members, init accessors and ref-returning methods have nothing to forward to. These are the ones the warning reports. See Ref struct parameters for the supported features.

A test usually checks one class, the system under test (SUT). The SUT talks to collaborators such as a database, a web service or a hardware device. A mock replaces such a collaborator: it implements the same interface (or derives from the same class), lets you decide what it returns, and records how it was called. Throughout this documentation the examples use this collaborator: IChocolateDispenser public delegate void ChocolateDispensedDelegate(string type, int amount); public interface IChocolateDispenser { int this[string type] { get; set; } int TotalDispensed { get; set; } bool Dispense(string type, int amount); event ChocolateDispensedDelegate ChocolateDispensed; } The mock is called dispenser, and the class that uses it is called sut: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); VendingMachine sut = new VendingMachine(dispenser); Pages that need further members declare them next to the example.

documents.t: The source generator adds a CreateMock() method to every type you mock. The returned object is an IChocolateDispenser, so you can pass it to your code directly. Everything that configures or inspects the mock is reached through its Mock property: Member Purpose Mock.Setup Decide how methods, properties and indexers behave. See Setup. Mock.Raise Raise events on the mock. See Events. Mock.Verify Check how the mock was used. See Verify interactions. Mock.SetupProtected, Mock.VerifyProtected, … The same for protected members of class mocks. See Protected members. Mock.SetupStatic, Mock.VerifyStatic, … The same for static interface members. See Static interface members. Mock.InScenario(…), Mock.TransitionTo(…) Switch between sets of setups. See Scenarios. Mock.Monitor(), Mock.ClearAllInteractions() Limit which interactions are counted. See Monitor interactions. Mock.As<T>() Reach an additional interface. See Create mocks. The generated setup and verification members mirror the members of the mocked type, so a typo or a wrong argument type is a compile error instead of a runtime exception.

Each call to the mock goes through the same steps: The call is recorded, so that you can verify it later. Mockolate looks for a matching setup. A setup matches when every argument satisfies its parameter matcher. If several setups match, the one defined last wins. The setup's callbacks run, and its return value or exception is used. Without a matching setup, the mock falls back to its MockBehavior: methods return a default value: false, 0, an empty string, an empty collection, a completed task, or null for other reference types; properties and indexers behave like normal storage: reading returns the value that was last written, or the default value if nothing was written yet; a mock created with ThrowingWhenNotSetup() throws a MockNotSetupException instead. dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("White", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(false); bool dark = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // true: only the first setup matches bool white = dispenser.Dispense("White", 1); // false: both match, the later one wins int before = dispenser.TotalDispensed; // 0: nothing was written yet dispenser.TotalDispensed = 5; int after = dispenser.TotalDispensed; // 5: the property stores the written value tip Define general setups first and more specific ones afterwards. Because the last matching setup wins, every dispenser.Mock.Setup.X statement starts a new setup that replaces earlier ones with the same arguments. Configure one setup by chaining: // ✔️ One setup: the property starts at 42 and logs every write dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .InitializeWith(42) .OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); // ❌ Two setups: the second one replaces the first, so the property starts at 0 dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); Class mocks A class mock also calls the base class implementation of a virtual member, even when a setup matches. The setup's return value takes precedence; the base class result is used only when no setup provides one. Use SkippingBaseClass() to turn the base class calls off.

documents.t: Verifications count the recorded interactions that match the given arguments and compare the count with your expectation. Nothing is checked until you call a count method such as .Once(), .Never() or .AtLeast(2); the Mockolate0001 analyzer warns you when you forget it. dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // passes dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // throws a MockVerificationException The exception message describes the expectation and what actually happened: Expected that mock invoked method Dispense(Milk, It.IsAny<int>()) exactly once, but it never did. Setups and verifications are independent: you can verify calls that have no setup, and a setup does not expect to be called. To check that every setup was used or every interaction was verified, see Check for unexpected interactions.
A complete example combines these concepts in one end-to-end test. The cheat sheet lists the most common calls on one page.
The most common calls at a glance. Follow the links for details. using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify;

The following example combines indexers, methods, events, stateful setup and verification into a single end-to-end scenario. The dispenser keeps track of its stock in the indexer, and every successful Dispense call reduces the stock and raises the ChocolateDispensed event: using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify; public delegate void ChocolateDispensedDelegate(string type, int amount); public interface IChocolateDispenser { int this[string type] { get; set; } int TotalDispensed { get; set; } bool Dispense(string type, int amount); event ChocolateDispensedDelegate ChocolateDispensed; } // Create a mock of IChocolateDispenser IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); // Setup: initial stock of 10 for Dark chocolate dispenser.Mock.Setup["Dark"].InitializeWith(10); // Setup: Dispense decreases the stock if there is enough, and returns true/false dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns((type, amount) => { int current = dispenser[type]; if (current >= amount) { dispenser[type] = current - amount; dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed(type, amount); return true; } return false; }); // Track the dispensed amount via the event int dispensedAmount = 0; dispenser.ChocolateDispensed += (type, amount) => { dispensedAmount += amount; }; // Act: try to dispense chocolates bool gotChoc1 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 4); // true bool gotChoc2 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 5); // true bool gotChoc3 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 6); // false, only 1 left // dispensedAmount == 9, dispenser["Dark"] == 1 // Verify: check the interactions dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Exactly(3); dispenser.Mock.Verify["Dark"].Set(It.IsAny<int>()).Twice(); The individual features are described in detail on the following pages: Create mocks Setup of methods, properties, indexers and events Parameter matching Verify interactions

You can create mocks of interfaces, classes and delegates. The source generator adds a static CreateMock() method to every type you mock. Example types used on this page Besides IChocolateDispenser, this page uses: public abstract class ChocolateDispenser { public abstract bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } public class MyChocolateDispenser : IChocolateDispenser { // a real implementation of IChocolateDispenser } public interface ILemonadeDispenser { bool DispenseLemonade(int amount); } // Create a mock of an interface IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); // Create a mock of a class ChocolateDispenser classMock = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); For classes without a parameterless constructor, pass the constructor arguments as an array: public abstract class ChocolateDispenserWithCtor(string defaultType, int capacity) { public abstract bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } ChocolateDispenserWithCtor classMock = ChocolateDispenserWithCtor.CreateMock(["Dark", 42]); info A class mock overrides the virtual and abstract members of the class. Non-virtual members cannot be intercepted and always run the real implementation. Sealed classes cannot be mocked; the Mockolate0002 analyzer reports this at compile time.

You can pass the setups directly to CreateMock. These setups are applied before the constructor of a class mock runs, so they also apply to virtual members that the constructor calls: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(setup => { setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(0); }); The setup callback can be combined with a MockBehavior and with constructor arguments in the same call.

A MockBehavior controls what the mock does when no setup matches. MockBehavior.Default returns default values and calls the base class implementation of class mocks (see Core concepts). Change it with the fluent -ing methods: // Throw a MockNotSetupException for every call without a matching setup IChocolateDispenser strictMock = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); // Combine a behavior with constructor arguments MockBehavior behavior = MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup(); ChocolateDispenserWithCtor classMock = ChocolateDispenserWithCtor.CreateMock(behavior, ["Dark", 42]); MockBehavior is an immutable record, so every method returns a new instance and you can safely share one behavior between many mocks and tests: MockBehavior strict = MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup(); IChocolateDispenser dispenser1 = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(strict); ILemonadeDispenser dispenser2 = ILemonadeDispenser.CreateMock(strict); Option Default Purpose ThrowingWhenNotSetup() off Throws a MockNotSetupException when no matching setup is found, instead of returning a default value. SkippingBaseClass() off Class mocks no longer call the base class implementation; without a setup they return a default value instead. SkippingInteractionRecording() off Interactions are not recorded. Setups, return values, callbacks and base class calls still work, but every verification throws a MockException. Useful in performance-sensitive scenarios. WithDefaultValueFor<T>(…) sensible defaults Customizes the default value for type T (see below). Initialize<T>(…) - Applies the given setups to every mock of type T created with this behavior. UseConstructorParametersFor<T>(…) - Default constructor arguments for mocks of class T, used unless you pass explicit arguments to CreateMock([…]). The Func<object?[]> overload creates them anew for each mock.

When no setup matches, the mock returns: an empty collection for collection types (e.g. IEnumerable<T>, List<T>), an empty string for string, a completed task for Task, Task<T>, ValueTask and ValueTask<T>, a tuple with recursively defaulted values for tuples, default(T) for value types and null for other reference types. You can register custom factories per type using .WithDefaultValueFor<T>(): MockBehavior behavior = MockBehavior.Default .WithDefaultValueFor<string>(() => "default") .WithDefaultValueFor<int>(() => 42); IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(behavior); For full control, implement IDefaultValueGenerator and pass it to the MockBehavior(IDefaultValueGenerator) constructor.

Use .Implementing<T>() to create a mock that also implements further interfaces: // A ChocolateDispenser that also implements ILemonadeDispenser ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Implementing<ILemonadeDispenser>(); // With setups for the additional interface IChocolateDispenser dispenser2 = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock() .Implementing<ILemonadeDispenser>(setup => setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true)); Use Mock.As<T>() to reach the Setup and Verify members of the additional interface: dispenser.Mock.As<ILemonadeDispenser>().Setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.As<ILemonadeDispenser>().Verify.DispenseLemonade(5).Once(); When the mock is already typed as the additional interface, its own Mock property reaches the same members, so you can skip As<T>(): ((ILemonadeDispenser)dispenser).Mock.Setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); All interfaces share the same mock: recorded interactions, scenario state and setups apply to every view of it. warning .Implementing<T>() returns a new mock instead of changing the one it was called on. Keep the returned reference; the original one does not implement T. Only the first type can be a class; additional types must be interfaces. Mock.As<T>() throws a MockException when the mock does not implement T, for example because it was not created with .Implementing<T>(). On class mocks, .Implementing<T>() reuses the constructor arguments the mock was created with. When the class already implements the interface .Implementing<T>() is also useful when the mocked class itself implements T, because it makes non-virtual members that the class implements mockable through the interface: public interface ICalculator { int Add(int a, int b); int Multiply(int a, int b); } public abstract class Calculator : ICalculator { public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b; // not virtual public abstract int Multiply(int a, int b); } Calculator calculator = Calculator.CreateMock().Implementing<ICalculator>(); // `Multiply` is overridable, so the class and the interface share one member: // either surface configures it, and both calls are recorded against it. calculator.Mock.Setup.Multiply(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(7); int viaClass = calculator.Multiply(3, 4); // 7 int viaInterface = ((ICalculator)calculator).Multiply(3, 4); // 7 // `Add` is not virtual, so only the call through the interface can be intercepted. calculator.Mock.As<ICalculator>().Setup.Add(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(99); int addViaClass = calculator.Add(1, 2); // 3, the real implementation int addViaInterface = ((ICalculator)calculator).Add(1, 2); // 99 Members hidden with new Mock.As<T>() also reaches a base interface whose members the mocked interface hides with new. No .Implementing<T>() is needed, because the base interface is already part of the mocked type. Methods, properties and events stay separate members, each with its own setups and recorded interactions: public interface IChocolateShelfBase { int Restock(); } public interface IChocolateShelf : IChocolateShelfBase { new int Restock(); } IChocolateShelf shelf = IChocolateShelf.CreateMock(); shelf.Mock.Setup.Restock().Returns(42); shelf.Mock.As<IChocolateShelfBase>().Setup.Restock().Returns(43); int viaDerived = shelf.Restock(); // 42 int viaBase = ((IChocolateShelfBase)shelf).Restock(); // 43 shelf.Mock.Verify.Restock().Once(); shelf.Mock.As<IChocolateShelfBase>().Verify.Restock().Once(); Indexers are the exception: they are keyed by their parameter signature rather than by the declaring interface, so a new indexer and the base indexer it hides share the same storage.

Use .Wrapping(instance) to forward all calls to a real object while still recording them, like a spy: MyChocolateDispenser realDispenser = new MyChocolateDispenser(); IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Wrapping(realDispenser); // The call is forwarded to the real instance dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 5); // You can still verify interactions dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).Once(); Both interface and class types can be wrapped. Setups take precedence over the wrapped instance, so you can still override individual members. Interface members are forwarded through the interface that declares them. This also covers members that hide a base member with new, and same-named members declared by several base interfaces. Protected members are not forwarded; the base class implementation is used instead. Init-only properties are not forwarded, since the wrapped instance is already constructed.

Mockolate generates its mocks with C# 14 extension members, so you need the .NET 10 SDK to build your tests. Your test projects can still target any supported framework: .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8, .NET 10 or .NET Framework 4.8. note If your test project pins <LangVersion>, it must be 14 or later (or latest).

.NET CLI PackageReference dotnet add package Mockolate <PackageReference Include="Mockolate" Version="*" /> Replace * with the latest version. Mockolate works with every test framework (xUnit, NUnit, MSTest, TUnit, …). The package contains the source generator and the analyzers, so there is nothing else to configure.

Suppose your code depends on a chocolate dispenser: Production code public interface IChocolateDispenser { bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } public class VendingMachine(IChocolateDispenser dispenser) { public string Buy(string type, int amount) => dispenser.Dispense(type, amount) ? "Enjoy!" : "Sold out"; } To test VendingMachine without a real dispenser, create a mock of IChocolateDispenser, tell it how to behave, and check afterwards how it was used: Test using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify; // Arrange: create the mock and set up its behavior IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); VendingMachine sut = new VendingMachine(dispenser); // Act string result = sut.Buy("Dark", 4); // Assert: result is "Enjoy!", and the dispenser was called exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 4).Once(); CreateMock() is generated for every type you mock, so IntelliSense shows it as soon as you type IChocolateDispenser.. Every mock has a Mock property that gives access to Setup, Verify and Raise. It.IsAny<int>() is a parameter matcher. Plain values like "Dark" match by equality. .Once() throws a MockVerificationException when the call count does not match. It lives in the Mockolate.Verify namespace. tip If you use aweXpect, the aweXpect.Mockolate extension lets you write verifications as awaitable expectations: await That(dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 4)).Once();.

A Roslyn analyzer and code-fix provider that migrates Moq and NSubstitute usage to Mockolate. Drop the package into a project that uses one of those libraries and the analyzer flags each mock it can migrate; the accompanying code fix rewrites the setup, verification, and event APIs to their Mockolate equivalents.

Install the NuGet package into the project you want to migrate: dotnet add package Mockolate.Migration The package only needs to be referenced while you are migrating — it ships the analyzer and code fixer, not runtime code. Once the source library is gone from a project you can remove the reference again.

After installing the package, every supported construct is reported as a warning. Apply the relevant code fix from your IDE (Visual Studio, Rider, VS Code with C# Dev Kit) or via dotnet format analyzers to rewrite the call site. Diagnostic Source library Code fix title MockolateM001 Moq Migrate Moq to Mockolate MockolateM002 NSubstitute Migrate NSubstitute to Mockolate The fixer rewrites the whole mock — the construction call, all setup calls on that mock, the corresponding verification calls, event wiring, and trailing .Object accesses (Moq) — in a single step.

The Moq fixer rewrites new Mock<T>(...) to T.CreateMock(...), drops every trailing .Object access, and moves setups and verifications onto the strongly-typed Mock.Setup / Mock.Verify chains. Strict mocks are mapped to MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup(), It.Is<T>(predicate) becomes It.Satisfies<T>(...), and event raising / verification are routed through Mock.Raise and event-specific Mock.Verify.<Event>.Subscribed() / Unsubscribed() calls. // Before (Moq) var mock = new Mock<IFoo>(); mock.Setup(m => m.Compute(It.IsAny<int>())).Returns(42); var sut = new Service(mock.Object); sut.Run(); mock.Verify(m => m.Compute(It.IsAny<int>()), Times.Once()); // After (Mockolate) var mock = IFoo.CreateMock(); mock.Mock.Setup.Compute(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(42); var sut = new Service(mock); sut.Run(); mock.Mock.Verify.Compute(It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // Before (Moq) — properties and events var mock = new Mock<IFoo>(MockBehavior.Strict); mock.SetupProperty(m => m.Name, "initial"); mock.Raise(m => m.Changed += null, EventArgs.Empty); mock.VerifyAdd(m => m.Changed += It.IsAny<EventHandler>(), Times.Once()); // After (Mockolate) var mock = IFoo.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); mock.Mock.Setup.Name.InitializeWith("initial"); mock.Mock.Raise.Changed(null, EventArgs.Empty); mock.Mock.Verify.Changed.Subscribed().Once();

The NSubstitute fixer rewrites Substitute.For<T>(...) to T.CreateMock(...) and reroutes the implicit setup/verify calls (sub.Method(args).Returns(...), sub.Received().Method(...)) through the strongly-typed Mock.Setup / Mock.Verify chains. Arg.Any<T>() becomes It.IsAny<T>(), Arg.Is<T>(predicate) becomes It.Satisfies<T>(...), and Raise.Event(...) is rewritten to the corresponding sub.Mock.Raise.<Event>(...) call. Nested-mock setups (sub.Child.M(args).Returns(...)) are migrated with a // TODO comment because the parent must be wired up to return the child mock manually. // Before (NSubstitute) var sub = Substitute.For<IFoo>(); sub.Compute(Arg.Any<int>()).Returns(42); var sut = new Service(sub); sut.Run(); sub.Received(1).Compute(Arg.Any<int>()); // After (Mockolate) var sub = IFoo.CreateMock(); sub.Mock.Setup.Compute(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(42); var sut = new Service(sub); sut.Run(); sub.Mock.Verify.Compute(It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // Before (NSubstitute) — sequential returns, When/Do, events var sub = Substitute.For<IFoo>(); sub.Compute(0).Returns(1, 2, 3); sub.When(x => x.Reset()).Do(_ => counter++); sub.Changed += Raise.EventWith(EventArgs.Empty); // After (Mockolate) var sub = IFoo.CreateMock(); sub.Mock.Setup.Compute(0).Returns(1).Returns(2).Returns(3).Forever(); sub.Mock.Setup.Reset().Do(() => counter++); sub.Mock.Raise.Changed(null, EventArgs.Empty);

NSubstitute's Returns(call => …), When(...).Do(call => …), and AndDoes(call => …) callbacks receive a CallInfo parameter that exposes the invocation arguments. Mockolate's equivalent overloads instead take the method's parameters directly, so the migration rewrites the lambda: Body never reads the parameter — drop it: Do(call => x++) → Do(() => x++). Body uses statically resolvable accesses (call.ArgAt<T>(literalIndex), call[literalIndex], or type-unique call.Arg<T>()) — rewrite the lambda's parameter list to match the receiver method and replace each access with the matching parameter name: Returns(call => call.ArgAt<int>(0) + 1) → Returns((int x) => x + 1). Anything else — bare call, dynamic indices, indexer-write for out/ref, ambiguous call.Arg<T>(), or local variables that would shadow the injected parameter names — preserve the original lambda and emit a // TODO comment so the rewrite can be done by hand.
